en: Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhìràn of the Tang Dynasty.
Regarding the explanation of the "profound realm" following the section on "all phenomena":

this is the fundamental principle of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the primary beginning of all teachings, the pivotal point for interpreting their meaning, and the refuge for sentient beings. It brings forth...

The reliance of the mind and the functional essence of expedient means; the root-source of delusion and awakening, and the fundamental principle of the fruit-virtue; the exhaustive reach of the single transformation and the ultimate conclusion of the five periods—by attaining these ten meanings, one eliminates all divergent views and becomes serene and free from error. Thus, one first praises the wisdom that relies [upon the Dharma], which is precisely the provisional and the real of the five Buddhas.
Upon what do the provisional and the ultimate rely?
It is that which is called the wondrous object (*viṣaya*).

If the object does not correspond to wisdom, it is not even the Buddha-wisdom; how much less can one understand this inconceivable wondrous wisdom by simply speaking of "confrontation" with respect to a non-existent object? For this reason, I have extensively refuted the various masters.

Next is the extensive establishment [of the doctrine]. The *Xuánzàn* and the *Zhǐguān* take this as their primary focus; among the vast and rich applications of meaning within our school, there are none that do not derive from this. Fearing that later generations might still lose their way back to it, I have been diligent and repetitive in my efforts. Yet, even those who personally seek out these teachings remain muddled about them.
Therefore, you must reflect upon this!
You must reflect upon this!
If one is deluded regarding this meaning, the pathways of all the teachings will spontaneously lose their direction, and the streams of the entire dispensation will here dry up.

Guangzhai says that "three times three" refers to the causes of persons, teachings, and conditions; because there was no meaning of a fruit in the past, each of the three vehicles has its own three, yet the single principle is not void.

Regarding the term "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): it should be understood as "real" because it is not false, and "reality" because its lack of characteristics constitutes its characteristic; thus it is called true reality.

As for the statement that "among the 'Four Ones,' only the Principle is singled out," according to the intention of Guangzhai, he shared the view of the older masters who did not establish a "unity of principle. He merely stated that principle is the foundation of the four ones, and therefore all four are called "one. This does not reach the meaning of the present text, which speaks of "the one among the four."
The passage ending with "this having been said" and the section on the "Northern Master" are both the interpretations of Guangzhai.

Regarding the statement "the Bodhisattva takes the six perfections as its essence," Guangzhai also established the Bodhisattva of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* as the Bodhisattva among the Three Vehicles; this refers precisely to the Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka in the present text.

Since recent times, this principle has been entirely discarded; the collection of the five hundred [arhats] must be traced back to the Five Indias. If one merely seeks to reconcile the regression [of the śrāvakas], yet claims that the Great [Vehicle] naturally takes refuge in the Buddha while the Way is unrelated to this, then not only would those of fixed nature be eternally extinguished, but even the Bodhisattvas would be engaged in empty talk.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it should be clarified that the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas take the conditions of the Truths (*satya-pratyaya*) as their essence.

As for the statement, "The actual objects are four, yet one; by means of the four, one principle is expanded," the four—namely causes, conditions, and so forth—are determined as the actual objects; therefore, through these, the single principle is extensively expounded.

Master Chang merely asserts that, according to the Buddha’s supreme teaching, there is only one reality and no three provisional means; while this principle is not without merit when contrasted with the Ten Powers, it falls short when compared to the current fourfold interpretation of the Buddha-vehicle, for even one of these interpretations is not yet exhaustive, as it lacks the ultimate [realization of] emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Among these, "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) is a general enumeration of the characteristics of the ten powers (*daśabala*); next, "nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth take their essential substance as the fundamental; finally, that which is called "general" (*sāmānya*) explains the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) in relation to the first eight powers, thereby subsuming the preceding nine through both the root and its branches.

Regarding the statement, "The various explanations above are not of a single path": these various explanations can be seen to each obtain only a small portion of the ten realms and ten suchnesses according to the present school’s interpretation; therefore, they are called "a single path."
Although Guangzhai seems to have attained the four sages for himself, he establishes only nine stages; furthermore, he divides the ninth and fifth stages into provisional and real.

Although the two masters Beiyao established all ten stages, they did not provide such distinctions; they remained within the framework of the three vehicles and lacked even a single stage of ultimate reality.

Now, since you have already accepted that the various Śākyas possess both the three vehicles and the one vehicle—and that each of these three and one possesses the ten aspects such as nature (svabhāva) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa)—why do you not also speak of the ten aspects of the six destinies?
The four noble beings represent the progression from cause to fruit; the six realms of existence should likewise be understood as both the phenomena and their corresponding [realms].

Since cause and fruit are identical, how could the ten meanings be lacking? The four noble beings are the illuminator, while the six realms are the illuminated; the ten realms are the illuminated, while the Buddha-vehicle is the illuminator. Therefore, the Buddha-wisdom illuminates the ten realms and the ten suchnesses, fully encompassing the three truths.

The principle of "ultimate equality" is perfectly clear; for what reason, then, do the various Buddhas each rely on a single path, thereby causing the Buddha's realm and wisdom not to be fully complete?
Now, the Master is unable to provide a detailed refutation, but merely offers a general critique of Guangzhai, stating that "the logic and text are inconsistent," and so forth.

"Principle" (li) refers to the underlying logic, while "text" (wen) refers to the manifest words; the initial text is evident, whereas in the subsequent refutation of the principle, one first employs four or five of the ten points to raise counter-objections.
Regarding "cause and effect": the causal conditions are the cause, and the retributive fruit is the effect.

From the phrase "if it were real" onwards, the refutation is addressed to persons based on four or five [realms]; however, according to the present text, one should discuss existence and non-existence by means of the ten realms.
Next, the section beginning with "The meaning is not... concludes the refutation. The text states: "All dharmas must encompass the ten realms;

within each realm, there are the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*). True reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is the essence of these realms and their suchnesses. If there were only one [suchness] and merely four [realms], then even outside that essence, five and nine would still be omitted; how much more so when every ten [realms] are all suchness?"
Now, wishing to provide a correct interpretation, I shall first cite the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), which was utilized by Dharmatrāta.
The purpose of citing this treatise is merely to provide a general analogy; it does not represent the exact same position.

Since the *Śāstra* states that each and every dharma possesses nine aspects, we know that Guangzhai should not judge them by distinguishing four or five categories, nor should the various masters rely on three or one respectively. Thus, it is clear that if one relies solely upon the ten realms and ten dharmas, the positions of all schools will collapse; how much more so when this fourfold interpretation is preeminent throughout antiquity and modernity? Only by interpreting the text in this manner does one accord with the intent of the Sūtra—where, then, do the logical principles of the various masters' divisions lie?

This Dharmottara is the author of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*; Dharmatrāta is a master mentioned in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, who was the successor of the author of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*. He is named after his teacher.

Since I have followed the *Mahā-śāstra* without making separate divisions, I have now stated in every single phrase that it corresponds to such characteristics as those found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; even if I do not provide exhaustive detail, this shall avoid the aforementioned errors.

Next, within the "Correct Explanation" section following "Now, to clarify," there are three parts: first, the restatement of the headings; second, the actual explanation, which consists of three points:
(1) listing the headings, (2) citing sacred words as evidence, and (3) the actual explanation.

In the cited passage, the first two sections are clear. Regarding the subsequent citation from the section on "separating and combining," which says, "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak," and so forth: because these ten dharmas—whether applied to oneself or to others—are realized only by the Buddha, it is said, "My Dharma is subtle and inconceivable."

However, while the cited texts primarily accord with the literal meaning, they also incorporate the sense of transcendence; since it is stated that only that which is "inconceivable" can universally accommodate all capacities, transcendence must be included.

Regarding the citation from the section on stages which says, "Only Buddhas and Buddhas are equal," this is because the ultimate principle of the three virtues is not something known by those on the seven preparatory stages.
Although one may not know the inherent nature (*dharmatā*) of these various stages, the ten [categories] are nonetheless divided according to their different affiliations.
Regarding the three-part formal explanation: first, within the initial ten realms, there are ten sections:

(1) the preliminary enumeration; (2) from "Even though the dharmas... onwards, the inclusion of dharmas within the realm-as-such (*dharmatā*); (3) from "As in the case of hell... onwards, the demonstration of their characteristics; (4) from "Therefore, according to the *Abhidharma*... onwards, using the small to illustrate the large; (5) from "One should know... onwards, using reason to infer the existence of the realm-as-such; and (6) from "If it illuminates... onwards, the final judgment.

Regarding the term "one's own station" (*svabhūmi*): although it clarifies that each of the ten realms contains ten within itself, it specifically illuminates one's own realm by treating the nine others as provisional (*upāya*) and the one as real (*tattva*). Therefore, it must be concluded that "within one there are immeasurable; one realm possesses ten. Each of these tens is suchness (*tathatā*); whether self or other, cause or fruit, they reside within a single mind. Thus, it is said that "within the immeasurable there is one, and within one there is the immeasurable. It cannot be described as one, nor can it be described as many; it cannot be described as provisional, nor can it be described as real. Whether cause or fruit, good or evil, empty or existent, great or small, ordinary being or sage, gradual or sudden, opening or closing, the mental phenomena, the environment and its inhabitants, or the one and the many—they are all sovereignly free. All dharmas are entirely like this.

Thus we know that those who discourse on the Dharma-realm have not yet exhausted its subtlety, which leads them to become confused about the facts of the effects of delusion and to remain lost regarding the principle of the causes.

7. From "If one illuminates the six realms" onwards, [the text] simultaneously refutes the Guangzhai school; since the Guangzhai school does not admit the ten realms, I shall now provisionally refute it based upon their own position.
Even if one were to maintain that each of the ten realms possesses its own ten suchnesses, these would still be merely the objects of discursive thought within their respective divisions.
This is all the more so in the case of Guangzhai, who asserts that there are only four types of noble beings, differing in four or five ways.
8. The section beginning with "The reason why" concludes the stages; first, it re-establishes the objective realm by stating, "the infinite within the one.

Regarding the phrase "Ordinary beings are cut off from principle," etc.: they say "cut off from principle" because they personally despise themselves as having no share [in this realization]; they say "deluded in emotion" because they follow their perceptions and hold divergent views. Since they are both cut off and deluded, what benefit is there in merely possessing [such a state]?

Regarding the phrase "the two vehicles" and so forth: this refers to the two vehicles of the two teachings; as for the three paths, one abandons them and does not contemplate them, avoiding emptiness while seeking emptiness, which conversely only serves to support the liberation of the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "Bodhisattvas" and so forth: the *zang* (Tripitaka) and *tong* (Shared) teachings illuminate the six stages, while the *bie* (Distinct) teaching illuminates them in sequence; thus it is said they are "not all-encompassing. All of these are deluded regarding their own realm and fail to reach the Buddha-realm. Although the term "not clearly" (*buliao*) still encompasses up to the tenth stage, one should now specifically point to the distinct stages and the causal grounds.

Regarding "endowed with both horizontal and vertical": within one there are immeasurables, which is the horizontal; immeasurables are themselves one, which is the vertical. Because the many and the one are mutually identical, they are said to be "endowed."
9. "Only" and below cite scriptural evidence; the concluding intent is as stated in the text. 10.

"The above *Xuanyi*" and below point to the extensive version; it is fully detailed in the *Xuanyi* text at the end of the "Excellence of the Realm" (*Jingmiao*), which says: "If expanded, it fills the Dharma-realm; one does not know from where it comes."
"When gathered, they are not known where they are; one does not know from where they have departed.
This refers to the extensive explanation of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses within the Dharma-realm.

Next, the Buddha-realm is treated in four parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the praise beginning with "This is endowed with..."; third, the analogical explanation beginning with "By analogy, it is also..."; and fourth, the conclusion by citing the fruit and the reproof beginning with "The Tathāgata..."
Question:
What is the distinction between the Buddha-realm mentioned here and the Buddha-realm among the ten previously mentioned?
Answer:

Previously, [the teaching] encompassed both delusion and its causes, as well as awakening and its fruits; now, it pertains solely to the fruit and does not extend to the causes or delusions. Therefore, each and every dharma employs "double negation": it is neither characteristic nor provisional, yet it is neither non-characteristic nor empty. Although it issues from double negation, its intent resides in the Three Truths. The subsequent nine [sections] should be understood accordingly, up to the ultimate identity of the fundamental and the derivative. Only in this way can it be called the ultimate Buddha-vehicle; therefore, all are concluded with the passage on the great carts.
In the context of the text of this present chapter, this is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena belonging to the stage of Buddhahood;
in that preceding parable, it is the great carriage of adornment for reaching the site of enlightenment;
and in that past life, it is the shore where the Buddha of the ultimate fruit reveals the provisional to reveal the real.
In that Fundamental Gate, this is precisely the wondrous Dharma realized by the One who attained Buddhahood long ago.

If the True Teaching can be understood, how could one be confused regarding its Dissemination? Even a single phrase or a single verse is utterly trustworthy; the discourse on the Three Virtues and the Three Tracks is as clear as if before one's eyes. If one grasps this meaning, then the extensive exposition over eight years does not transcend a single thought-moment, and the passage of fifty minor kalpas does not stir a single kṣaṇa.

Know that within a single lifetime, the accommodation of capacities resides within the nature of mind; the Buddha-activities of the ten directions are clearly before one's eyes, and the fundamental natures of the dharma-realm are easily understood upon inspection. All teachings spoken according to what is appropriate point directly to the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Regarding the summary critique that uses the eye as an analogy: for the time being, let us discuss the "one eye" obtained by those of the Hīnayāna who perceive emptiness with their wisdom-eye. From the Bodhisattva of the first stage up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there still remains ignorance; now, this critique specifically addresses those Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who have not yet seen the Middle Way, comparing them all to one seeing at night.

Next, the explanation of the "separating and combining" is divided into four parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the praise of the object under the heading "separating"; third, the censure under the heading "ordinary beings"; and fourth, the conclusion under the heading "for this reason."
The initial section consists of three parts, namely the three statements;
these can be seen by carefully examining the present sutra according to their respective contexts.
The fourth section concerns only the two [truths] of the Middle Way.
First, the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*) are explained; next, from "the initial stage" onwards, the ultimate [nature] and so forth are explained again.
Regarding the first passage, the triad of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), nature (*svabhāva*), and substance (*dravya*) differs slightly from the previously mentioned Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*).

The previous section clarified that [the Buddha] has already attained the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, the ten dharmas were presented through a discussion of the contrast between cultivation and nature.

This present section clarifies that the stages involve both the holy and the ordinary; thus, the ten dharmas are categorized according to these stages. Because the ten dharmas correspond to distinct stages, it is said here to be "according to the stages."

The first three [perfections] pertain exclusively to the stage of principle and are definitively situated within the rank of ordinary beings; their power resides in the five stages, and their activity resides in the six sense organs. The conditions and causes refer to the acquired "conditions" and "understanding" attained from the first stage upward; the retributive fruit refers to the ultimate fruits of Bodhi and Nirvana.
Bodhi is the fruit;
Nirvana is the retribution.

Therefore, although the first three [categories] are generally listed among the ten realms, the three virtues within each realm are co-present within the fundamental nature (li-xing). Consequently, even the term "ten realms" refers exclusively to the level of principle.
If this were not the case, why would it say, "If one investigates these ten realms," and so forth?
Therefore, the textual evidence for the three virtues of the rational nature (li-xing) is found here.

However, in many passages, the discussion frequently proceeds by contrasting the cultivated (xiu) and the inherent (xing), which is done for the purpose of establishing the characteristics of the teachings.
The reader should understand this.
Upon seeing this text, one should realize that it synthesizes all the preceding explanations.

From "If one investigates" up to "such a karmic retribution," the first three dharmas—being both within the nature and within the cause—are collectively termed "correct. Therefore, from "power" (*bala*) onwards belongs to cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and to the fruit (*phala*). Thus, from the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) onward, one investigates this objective realm of the nature; there is the power to eliminate coarse afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as the performance of practices that resemble [the ultimate] realization.

If one enters the stage of partial realization, the union of these three with that nature is termed "correct"; then, being endowed with the auxiliary factors, they are termed "causes and conditions. Upon reaching the ultimate stage, enlightenment is termed the "fruit" and nirvana is termed the "recompense."

Although these are divided to correspond to the beginning and the end, they constitute the single stage of cause and effect within the Buddha’s Dharma-realm; therefore, this differs from the ancients’ method of categorizing them as provisional and real. Regarding the phrase "the first three" and so forth:

"first" refers to the three dharmas within the causal stage, such as the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic), while "last" refers to the three dharmas on the resultant ground within the *vipāka* (fruition). Thus, one knows that the three virtues are identical to the three truths; hence it is said, "from the beginning and the end... to the ultimate equality."
The section "The Initial Stage" below provides a further detailed explanation of the ultimate state, which is divided into two parts:
the exposition and the conclusion.
Within the exposition, there are three sections:
First, it re-explains that the three virtues are non-dual in their essence and manifestation, concluding with the state beyond praise;
second, it re-explains that ultimate equality constitutes non-duality;
third, it explains the inconceivable.

First, regarding the explanation of the three virtues: "Evil" refers to the three evil [paths]; "Good" refers to the three good [paths]; "Worthy" refers to the lesser worthies; "Sage" refers to the lesser sages; "Small" refers to the lesser among the intermediate worthies and sages; and "Great" refers to the various great stages.
Regarding the re-explanation of "ultimate equality" and so forth, there are again three parts:

first, establishing the objects within the context of delusion; second, from the words "If one is deluded," onward, contrasting the three truths in terms of delusion and awakening; third, from the words "Furthermore, regarding the provisional and the real," onward, discussing them in terms of persons and teachings.

Regarding these four interpretations: the first clarifies that the principle encompasses all by interpreting it in terms of the ten realms; the second clarifies the ultimate self-realization by interpreting it in terms of the Buddha-realm; the third clarifies the Buddha’s transformative function by interpreting it through the categories of separation and union; and the fourth clarifies the pervasiveness of the three virtues by interpreting them across all stages.

If one considers the breadth or narrowness of the mutual application of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), there are four interpretations: first, if one possesses all four explanations, then this [the former] is broad while that [the latter] is narrow; second, if this refers only to the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*) without mentioning the three thousandfold world, then this is narrow while that is broad. Although the terminology may differ, the principle must necessarily be equal: the cause must possess the fruit, and the primary [retribution] must necessarily have its support.

However, within the original *Śāstra*, the explanation of these ten suchnesses exhausts the principle and reaches the ultimate limit of the teaching; I shall now set forth the purport of the *Śāstra* so that it may harmonize with the doctrinal intent of our own school. The *Śāstra* states: "It is accomplished and cannot be fully described."
"True reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to the fact that the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha-Dharmakāya is unchanging; thus, the Buddha's wisdom fully knows this substantial reality.
Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* that says "such characteristics" and so forth, the *Śāstra* asks:
"What is this dharma?"
What is the phenomenon? What is it like?
What are its characteristics?
What is the substance of phenomena?
What are phenomena? They refer to the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Why are they called phenomena? Because they arise as various things and are thus explained.
As for what constitutes the nature of the Dharma, it is because one attains purity by relying on the three gates.
As for what constitutes the characteristic of the Dharma, it is because the meaning of the three kinds is the single-characteristic Dharma.
As for what constitutes the essence of the Dharma, it is because there is only the single Buddha-vehicle without any difference.
Now, it is said that the first phrase first clarifies that the ten suchnesses (daśa-tathatā) are common to the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
The second phrase refers to the "Three Vehicles" themselves, because of the differences in their teachings.
The third phrase refers to the persons of the Three Vehicles, who, relying on the teachings, accord with reality.
"The second phrase opens up the characteristics of the three vehicles, for there are no other characteristics.
The third phrase opens up the essence of the three vehicles, for it is solely the one reality.
The *Treatise* further states:
"What are the phenomena? They are conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. What kind of phenomena?
They are phenomena that arise from causes and conditions and phenomena that do not arise from causes and conditions.
What are phenomena like? They are permanent and impermanent phenomena."
As for the nature of phenomena (*lakṣaṇadharma*), it refers to the three characteristics such as arising, which are themselves the three characteristics such as non-arising.
As for the substance of phenomena (*svabhāvadharma*), it refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) being non-aggregates.
Now, it is said that this section departs from the three vehicles (*triyāna*) to provide a successive and distinct explanation that returns to the essence of the true mark (*lakṣaṇatathatā*).
Regarding the first phrase: it is because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the śrāvaka is contrasted with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena of the six realms of existence.
The second phrase is because the Pratyekabuddha is contrasted with others who are not [born] from causes and conditions.
The third phrase is because the Dharma of the Bodhisattva is contrasted with the other eight elements, all of which are impermanent.
The second phrase means that, in general, the three vehicles are contrasted with the remaining six realms because all possess the three characteristics.
The third phrase means that the ten realms and the five aggregates are all substantial entities.
The *Śāstra* further states:
"What is the nature of phenomena? It is that which is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.
What is the characteristic of phenomena? It refers to phenomena such as those possessing visible characteristics."
Regarding "the essence of phenomena": this refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which consist of the grasper and the grasped, and constitute the aggregate of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*).
Furthermore, these five aggregates are the essence of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

Now, it is said that this single section of commentary on the first two phrases is subsumed within the third phrase, and furthermore, the third is condensed into the fourth, because the teachings of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) are all visible therein.

Furthermore, by subsuming the fourth [truth] into the fifth, the initial truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are established; it further indicates that suffering and its origin are entirely comprised of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Thus it says: "Moreover, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the essence of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). Therefore, one knows that the six destinies and the three vehicles, when viewed from the perspective of ultimate reality, are still nothing but suffering and its origin.
The *Śāstra* further states:
"There is also a teaching based on reliance: what are the dharmas? They are the bodies of names, words, and phrases. Why are they called dharmas?
Because the Tathāgata relies upon them to teach the Dharma."
What is the nature of phenomena? It is that which can teach and transform sentient beings who are capable of being transformed.
What is the characteristic of phenomena? It is that which is apprehended by means of sound.
What is the substance of phenomena? It is the characteristic of the substance of phenomena as a provisional designation.
Now, this first interpretation is intended to explain the preceding [passage] by means of the teaching based upon the five phrases.
As for the first phrase, it fully elucidates the provisional and real dharmas of the ten realms.
The second phrase indicates that the basis [of the teaching] is entirely real, as there are no other teachings remaining.
The third phrase clarifies that sentient beings receive [the teaching] differently according to their distinct faculties, capacities, and conditions.
The fourth phrase clarifies that all faculties and conditions converge within the Great Transformation (Mahāparinirvāṇa).

The second phrase clarifies that the transformer and the transformed, as well as the signifier and the signified, are all provisional designations, because when compared to the signified, there is only the realization of reality.

One must know with faith that the text of the *Śāstra* cannot be judged hastily; thus, it is only by employing the present interpretation that one accords with the sublime intent. Moreover, the fourfold exegesis of the *Śāstra* is precisely the fourfold exegesis of our own school.
The first explanation, since it regards the essence and characteristics of the three vehicles as all being the single essence and characteristic, is the explanation in terms of the Buddha-realm.
The second explanation, since it explains the three vehicles in relation to the six destinies, is the explanation in terms of the ten realms.
The subsequent explanation, which correlates suffering and its origin with the Path and excludes anything else, is an explanation based on the stages [of practice].

The following explanation is based on the teaching that expresses [these meanings]; because the teachings are provisional or ultimate, there is the giving of assemblies, which is an analysis by way of both division and combination.

Thus we know that the great principles of this school are in perfect accord with the purport of the *Śāstra*; consequently, the eighteen phrases of the extant text constitute eighteen successive layers of explanation regarding the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*).
This treatise is so rich in content that few understand it; following the general discussion, I shall now provide a fourfold explanation.

Third, the section beginning with "If one proceeds from... explains the inconceivable (*acintya*). Although the preceding object has already been established as inconceivable, its name remains general; therefore, it is now further distinguished from the conceivable (*cintya*) so that one may recognize the first four explanations as the true inconceivable.
First, the essential characteristics are briefly presented; second, analogies from various instances are cited; third, the conclusion is reached by applying the underlying principle.
Regarding the first section, the essential characteristics are first presented in brief, and subsequently, the passage beginning with "various sūtras" points to the detailed exposition.
The initial passage first presents the doctrine and then provides an analogy.
Regarding the initial passage, it first explains the names:
it is "inconceivable" because it transcends the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), and it is "incomparable" because it lies beyond the path of language.
Next, the passage beginning with "unable to practice" defines the essential nature [of the state].
This essence is neither cause nor effect, nor is it that which proceeds toward a goal.
"Practice" (caryā) refers to the cause.
"Arriving" refers to the fruit (*phala*).
This essence (*svabhāva*) should not be categorized as either cause or fruit; if it were to belong to the capacity [of the cause], it would have no relation to the essence.
Next, an analogy is presented, consisting of three parts: the principle (*dharma*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*).

Regarding the first principle: one contemplates that form (*rūpa*) is permanent and therefore does not perish. What is permanent must necessarily possess the four [elements], and these four are simply the mind; the same applies to their non-differentiation. Within the analogies, there are two layers:

first, using light and darkness as metaphors for the fact that the inconceivable and delusion share the same essence, it is thus pointed out that the moonlight’s entirety of brightness is itself darkness.

Next, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, when the sun rises" uses the analogy of transforming darkness into light. As for the statement "it is ever-present," this simply means that darkness lacks the inherent nature of darkness; by pointing out the darkness, it is revealed as light. The same applies to delusion and awakening: their fundamental nature is no different.

Although it is currently said to be "non-existent," this is also not the same as the Kai-shan school, because it is spoken from the perspective after the attainment of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

Regarding "If they definitely exist," the following section refutes the attachment to their definite existence, fearing that one might reckon that even after three cycles there would still be śrāvakas.

Regarding "If they definitely do not exist," this refutes the fixed reckoning of non-existence; as seen at the beginning of the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta), where due to the light one sees Mañjuśrī being led away;

and at the beginning of the "Expedient Means Chapter" (Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta), where after the first cycle of the Dharma-discourse for the twelve hundred people was completed, they still did not awaken and remained dependent upon the parable-discourse.

In the text concerning past lives, there are those who currently abide on the stage of the śrāvaka; furthermore, it cites those who do not know, such as Śāriputra, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth, which is circulated everywhere.
Why do you say they do not exist?

Furthermore, when we speak of their non-existence, it is intended to refute the fixed view of those who abide in the fruits [of the path] that there is eternal extinction; it does not mean that they were originally non-existent.

The passage beginning with "If one says... is now a general challenge; although we have conceded that they truly exist as being led by the provisional, we still fear that others might use the Buddhas of the Tripiṭaka as an analogy.
"The principle here is not analogous," as stated in the following passage of the current text:
"When the Buddha abides at the pinnacle of fruition, there is no practice of actualization; the śrāvakas are not so, and therefore they possess it."
The words of the Buddha in the Tripiṭaka originate from the teachings of the present; therefore, we know that this is not a difficulty raised by another.
As for the phrase "in what place," since the Buddha must possess the perfection of the three bodies, this Buddha is designated as provisional (upāya).
If one says there are thirty-four minds, this is merely a provisional teaching that appears to be real.
Among scholars of past and present, even this Buddha would not dare to be considered provisional; who then would know that the site of enlightenment at Vajrāsana is not real?
The section beginning with "Now, it is clear" provides the formal explanation, first establishing the principle and then citing the treatise.

First, the brief establishment [of the argument] is given; next, regarding the passage beginning with "If one follows," since even in ultimate wisdom there is no Avīci hell, how could one see that Śrāvakas definitely exist?

If it is said that when the time has not yet arrived, there is meaning that is not erroneous, then the Elder [Śāriputra] had no Buddha-eye from beginning to end; yet, observing with the Dharma-eye, it must have been present in the interim. Furthermore, regarding his status as a person, this refers to the period prior to receiving his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Next, the citation of the treatise is divided into five parts: first, the direct citation of the treatise;

second, from "If based on" onwards, establishing five types by comparing the present sutra with the meaning of the treatise; third, from "If following" onwards, the judgment; fourth, from "If attained" onwards, the conclusion of the intent; and fifth, from "Furthermore" onwards, the judgment of the greatness.
The introductory commentary follows the text as it stands.
Next, our school, relying on the sutras and looking toward the treatises, merely adds the single category of the Buddha-way.

Regarding the third section on judgment, from "If from the perspective of certainty" to "the treasure place," although [retrogression] does not exist in the Mahāyāna, it still exists according to the Hīnayāna. Since those who have regressed from the bodhicitta still belong to the realm of existence, they are said to "regress from the Mahāyāna" because they were originally within the Hīnayāna teachings and we are now discussing their initial state.
The passage beginning with "As for the reality being thus" clarifies the manifestation through response and transformation (*nirmāṇa*).

That which is cited as the capacity to transform through the turning of the mind (*cittavivarta*) is fundamentally great; if one is included in neither of the two paths of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), it was not originally a matter of deliberation.
5. Regarding the section beginning with "Furthermore," which further distinguishes between the existence and non-existence of the Mahāyāna: first there is the distinction, followed by the conclusion.

The intended meaning is that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is considered non-existent [as a distinct vehicle], because both the fourth and fifth [bodies] are designated as "Great. Therefore, in the *Śāstra*, the term "Mahāyāna" does not appear; it merely refers to the "nirmāṇakāya."

The phrase "If one follows" below specifically refers to the Buddha-way; this employs the terminology established by our own school, yet in explaining its meaning through the "revealing of the origin," it still excludes the three vehicles, because once one has received the prediction, they are designated as a Bodhisattva who has attained patience within their birth-body (janmakāya).

Therefore, by taking up those who have revealed their origins, we know that they possess a real foundation and may also be called Mahāyāna śrāvakas; thus, from the perspective of their concealed virtue they are non-existent, but from the perspective of their revealed origins they exist.

The reason they receive the title of "Mahāyāna Śrāvaka" is that, while manifesting their original departure [from the Lesser Vehicle], they still demonstrate themselves as śrāvakas; thus, they are so named.
This differs from other interpretations which posit the existence of śrāvakas within the Mahāyāna itself.

From the passage "Now opening for three" onwards, the formal text’s primary intent must be understood as being directed toward two types of individuals. For those who have regressed from the Great Vehicle, this is no different from what is stated in the *Treatise* (*Śāstra*). However, the definitive meaning here appears slightly distinct: while the *Treatise* bases its account on those present in the assembly receiving their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), the present text bases its account on the general principle of the opportunity being opened. Thus, it includes those not present in the assembly who transmit the teaching to others, or those outside the boundary who also hear it, or those who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, are exhorted and compelled to believe; this sutra speaks generally, simply stating "granted a prediction."

The *Śāstra* states that the retrogression from the Mahāyāna is based on one particular perspective; for instance, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, who could have known that the various Śrāvakas would regress from the Mahāyāna?
At assemblies such as those of the *Vaipulya* sūtras, they were all said to have extinguished their spiritual lineage.

According to the intent of the present sutra, since both parties have heard the teaching, they must both receive its seal; once this is opened, there is no further discrepancy. One should distinguish between those who have turned back and those who have not as two distinct meanings; thus, one should know that the *Śāstra* involves a provisional statement and should not be equated with the definitive intent of the sutra.

Regarding the third point concerning the density or thinness of afflictions: the ancient masters explained "affliction" (*huo*) by means of "delusion" (*hui*), whereas the present masters explain "affliction" by means of "troublesome delusion" (*fanhuo*); therefore, this differs from the former tradition.
Among these, the ancient interpretations are first presented.
It is called "wandering contemplation" (*yóuguān*) because one repeatedly contemplates what has been realized; through this wandering contemplation, one knows that the single principle is identical.
The section beginning with "As for... clarifies the cause of their delusion, which arises from differences in the teachings they have heard.
The phrase "it must be" (*jìng bì*) below correctly clarifies that mutual doubt gives rise to delusion.
Since the teaching fundamentally elucidates the principle, if the means of expression (*neng quán*) are three, how can that which is expressed (*suǒ quán*) be one?
If that which is expressed were one, how could the means of expression be three?
The phrase "hesitating" below clarifies the characteristics of his delusion; although he is still wandering in uncertainty, he has not yet distinguished between gain and loss.

The section beginning with "by means of principle" below judges his gain and loss: being deluded by principle while relying on the teaching results in the gain of conforming to principle; being deluded by the teaching while relying on principle results in the loss of contradicting principle.

Regarding the phrase "those of superior faculties" (*uttamendriya*) and so forth: this refers to the distinction between the three cycles of entry into the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), which is determined by the gains and losses regarding the principles and teachings of the Small and Middle Vehicles.

Thus, those of superior faculties have a strong inclination toward grasping a single principle; since this principle is termed "near to the Great," they hear that there are not three [vehicles] and accord with the single principle, and for this reason, they awaken first.

Regarding those deluded about principle, it is through the threefold hearing that one finally knows that the single principle is without deviation; thus, by means of this, those of inferior capacity achieve awakening.
As for those of middling capacity, because their two types of mental power are equal, their awakening resides in the middle.

The section beginning with "Now it is said" below is a refutation. First, there is a general refutation of their claim that mutual confusion regarding both principle and teaching serves as the three roots.
If these mutual confusions were indeed the three roots, then it would be impossible for such confusion to arise in advance before one has even heard the three cycles of teaching.

Next, following the section on the "three persons," the two points of the refutation are fully set forth: first, that the Great and Small Vehicles are eternally unrelated; second, that being within the Small Vehicle one should not be confused by the Great.
Within the initial of these two distinct refutations, there are further two parts; first, in order to establish the matter, it asks, "What [are they]? (何等).

Regarding the phrase "If one is distracted," the refutation below consists of two parts. First, it is refuted by way of the Lesser Vehicle: if doubt belongs to the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), then even the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) does not possess it; how then can mutual doubt be designated as one of the three roots?
Next, the passage beginning with "If one who is preoccupied with the Mahāyāna... addresses the refutation from the perspective of the Great [Vehicle].
Since the Great and Small [Vehicles] are distinct, how could one harbor mutual doubts regarding the principles and teachings of the Great Vehicle?

The subsequent intent is to apply the meaning of the present sutra: if there were mutual confusion regarding the principles and teachings of the Great and Small Vehicles, where would you have heard the refutation of the three [vehicles]?

Although the Vaipulya sūtras may criticize [the Lesser Vehicle] and the Prajñāpāramitā may supplement it, neither ever states that these three are merely expedient means; thus we know that prior to this, there was no confusion between the Great and Small Vehicles. How could there be any hesitation regarding the three aspects of entering, abiding in, and emerging from meditative contemplation?

The passage beginning with "Already having anticipated" below raises a hypothetical objection: since you have previously been led astray by both reasoning and scripture, it should be known that you have already shaken your convictions and given rise to doubt.

If such doubt had already arisen, you should have attained understanding through the brief opening of the three periods; how then could you, upon hearing this brief account, still say, "The fourfold assembly all harbor doubts"?
Regarding the phrase "on this day," it refers to the time when [the teaching] was briefly expounded as heard.
"Advancing and retreating" below concludes the refutation of errors.

Next, from "Now, I clarify" onwards is the formal explanation: first, the primary intent is determined; second, the three faculties are judged by means of four propositions; third, entering and abiding are elucidated by means of three grades.

Regarding the initial passage: first, it is generally explained that the faculties (*indriya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) differ from those of others; since in the Hīnayāna the faculties are fixed and the afflictions are further eliminated, how could one then proceed to analyze the afflictions according to the Hīnayāna?

Even though he may be deluded by the small regarding the great, he does not establish a separate name for such delusion; therefore, the minor delusions do not constitute a difference in degree of thickness.
Question:
Since there are no textual passages concerning the severance of distinct delusions prior to that point for the various Śrāvakas, why is it now discussed in terms of their thickness?
Answer:

Although this is not explicitly taught in the scriptures, it logically follows that it must exist; therefore, its meaning is that it is subject to elimination through refinement (*praśamana*). Because the faculties (*indriya*) are not equal, the methods of elimination and suppression (*prahāṇa-praśamana*) also differ, resulting in three types of faculties whose sequence is not uniform.
Next, regarding the four phrases, they are first listed and then individually correlated with the four types of people.

Since both faculties and afflictions arise from past habitual tendencies, resulting in three different cycles of awakening, there are three judgments: the first interpretation exhausts the scope of those to be guided; thus, the fourth phrase encompasses the assembly of those who have established a karmic connection.

Regarding the two subsequent explanations of indeterminacy: while the three faculties (*indriya*) are already established, the formal arrangement of the categories extends to four; since these four are used to judge the three, there is flexibility in advancing or retreating.

In the second explanation, the middle two phrases should be taken as the "middle" category. As for the text stating "for the middle and inferior," either the character "inferior" (*xià*) is redundant, or the term "inferior faculty" (*xiàgēn*) constitutes a separate phrase.
Regarding the third point, which concerns the three grades of delusions, there are two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the analogy.

First, as for the explanation: both stages consist of three layers. Here, we shall first clarify that at the beginning of the three cycles, upon entering the first dwelling (*prathamābhūmi*), there are three differences, precisely because the exhaustion of delusions is not uniform.

The phrase "For example" below uses a small case to illustrate the large: all sixteen moments are termed "untainted" (anāsrava); until the fifteenth moment, one still receives the name of a "candidate" (pratipannaka). Therefore, only when the three grades [of afflictions] are exhausted does one enter the first stage (prathama-bhūmi), at which point one finally receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa).
Regarding the fourth [point], "the transformation of faculties or non-transformation of faculties," it first restates the ancient view.

Next, the refutation beginning with "If that were so" argues that although there is the designation "transformation" because [the faculties] arise simultaneously with hearing, the three faculties are not established [as such].
If one turns [the wheel], the subsequent refutation shows that the meaning of "turning" is not established, and furthermore, the three faculties do not exist.
Since all instances of awakening during the three cycles are equally termed "superior," by what means would you distinguish between the three cycles and the three faculties?
Those others who have not yet awakened are not said to have undergone a transformation.
The subsequent analogy intends to show that if one first establishes a premise and then subjects it to critique,
yet both the benefit and the distinction between the sharp and dull faculties remain as before, this is not called a transformation.
“Śāriputra, upon hearing this once,” and so forth, is fully explained as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
Following that, from “Now, as for sentient beings” onwards, is the main exposition, which consists first of the formal explanation and secondly of the analytical discussion (*liaojian*).
The first section first cites the present as an analogy; since the present is transformed by conditions, it is verified that the past was likewise so.
The passage beginning with "In previous lives" clarifies that the three faculties were already transformed in prior births, which is why the three faculties lead to awakening and entry in succession.

Regarding the subsequent analogy: the blade is like the root, the wood is like delusion, and the wielder is like the trigger. The Buddha’s command to "cut" is like hearing the Dharma; the execution of the cut is like applying contemplation; the felling of the wood is like realization; and the prior whetting is like the turning [of the wheel]. Because the encounters with whetting differ, there are degrees of sharpness and dullness. Herein, hearing and awakening appear to be the practice of faith (*śraddhā-carita*), yet they are not devoid of the other methods. This is due to the differing ways in which faith and the Dharma mutually assisted one another during previous lives. The complete characteristics of faith and the other faculties are as described in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mo-ho chih-kuan).
Within this single sitting, there should not be sixty-four instances.

The meaning of the question is: before entering and abiding [in the meditative state], they are called the "three faculties"; once one has entered and abided therein, are these still called the "three" [faculties]?
The intent of the answer can be seen [in the preceding text].

The intent of the subsequent question is as follows: "That which precedes the first stage (*bhūmi*) is called 'conditioned' (*ālambana*), while the first stage itself is called 'real' (*tattva*). Since that which precedes the second stage is also called "conditioned cultivation" (*ālambana-bhāvanā*) before it is realized, if there are already gradations in the conditioned cultivation prior to the first stage, are there also gradations prior to the second stage?

The meaning of the answer is as follows: Since their stages and principles are identical, they should not be treated separately. While there may be differences prior to abiding because realization has not yet been attained, even those prior to the perfect stage (yuan-zhu) are called "those who take it as an object" (*yuán*). However, this applies only to those within this [teaching] and the four foundations of mindfulness; furthermore, their names are established based on the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*).
Regarding the five points on understanding and not understanding: first, the current text establishes its own position; second, it cites a scripture to raise an objection;
third, under the section beginning with "If one says," it presents the objection;
fourth, under "However, the scripture," it provides a discernment, hence it states: "The meaning is not necessarily so."
Therefore, in the past, the three faculties were not the same across the three turnings; with three turnings for each of the three vehicles, there are nine in total.
Regarding the phrase "In this present sutra" below, our school must now distinguish whether pratyekabuddhas exist or not; first, the text raises an inquiry to address potential objections.
It has already been established that the three faculties are present throughout all three vehicles; now, what passage in this sutra speaks of the pratyekabuddha’s awakening?
Below the section on "pratyekabuddhas," the author resolves this objection.
As for the term "middling faculty," it refers to the three vehicles mentioned previously.
Regarding the phrase "according to the faculties" (*mūla*), it is because within the Śrāvakas there are likewise three types of faculties.
The passage beginning with "Therefore, Śāriputra... serves as proof that there is no separate Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
Since it has been clarified that the two vehicles attain awakening through different faculties, the Bodhisattvas should also be present throughout all three cycles [of teaching]. Which ones are they?

Therefore, the former masters emerged to clarify that the Bodhisattvas’ awakening is permitted to possess three capacities (*indriya*), yet all of them spoke according to the Dharma [of the first turning] and did not reach the middle or lower two cycles.
As for the phrase "the domain of the mind" (*yu huai*): "domain" (*yu*) refers to a boundary or limit; it denotes the scope of one's directed intention.

Regarding the term "proximate fruit" (*upapanna-phala*): it refers to the stage of commonality (*sādhāraṇāvasthā*). This means that although one seeks to attain Buddhahood by departing from the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), the Buddha-fruit remains identical to the stage of the two vehicles; therefore, it is called "proximate fruit."

Now, hearing that the fruit of Buddhahood transcends five hundred [aeons], even if there remain doubts regarding its distance or proximity, it is not like the Lesser Vehicle and is thus easy to awaken to.
Regarding the "three faculties" below, ancient commentators judge that the three periods are all contained within the Dharma-exposition (dharmadeśanā).
The section beginning with "Now, to clarify" refutes [the objection].

Prior to the first cycle, in the initial reference to the Dharma-exposition and within the brief exposition, the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles occupy the foremost position; however, they do not all appear together at the very beginning.

"If that is so," the following passage cites scriptural evidence: how can it be that in the "Chapter on the Merits of Discernment" (*Vibhāga-guṇa-parivarta*) and in the sections on the Propagation of the Teaching, such as the "Chapter on the Wondrous Sound" (*Ghoṣadatta-parivarta*), there are still those who have only recently attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Regarding the phrase "The old [commentary] says," the ancient commentator’s intention was to claim that "in the first *kalpa*, one first realizes the already perfected Dharmakāya.
Regarding the phrase "Now it says," he again refutes this:
how could those six hundred and eighty billion [beings] have already been the Dharmakāya and yet still be said to have "attained the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Only after the attainment of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is one said to "increase the path.

Regarding the subsequent question: since it is not permitted that bodhisattvas exist solely during the first period, should the followers of the two vehicles likewise reach [the stage of] the "Life Span" chapter?
The intent of the answer is that "person" does not apply exclusively to the first [turning], while "name" does not extend to the subsequent ones.
Question:

Since one has already attained non-arising (*anutpāda*) within the three turnings, this is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); why then do you not accept the interpretation of the ancient masters?
Answer:

According to the intention of the ancient masters, he was originally a bodhisattva who attained the dharma-body upon hearing the Dharma during the first cycle; by the time of the "Life Span" chapter, he had increased his path and diminished his births.

Now, although it is said that śrāvakas ultimately become bodhisattvas, there may be some who have not yet attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti); since they cannot be said to be increasing their path, they are simply referred to as "non-arising."

Now, regarding the Master’s previous challenge to the ancients: originally, even a Bodhisattva must first reach that stage before attaining non-arising (anutpāda), as was previously explained in the section on "Contemplation" (*vimaṃsā*). First attaining the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth is itself one path; how could it be that all Bodhisattvas must necessarily attain non-arising prior to the teaching of the Dharma?

Therefore, we know that those of the two vehicles whose faculties and natures have attained prediction may also only attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) later on; thus, one must not generalize.
One should understand that all [teachings] apply to both the beginning and the end; it is simply that after the three weeks, the name "Lesser Vehicle" no longer exists.

Regarding the sixth section on understanding existence and non-existence: although it is not explicitly stated that this was an old view, such a calculation existed in antiquity; therefore, it is cited here for refutation.
From the words "Now, to clarify," the text first refutes the pratyekabuddhas and subsequently distinguishes the bodhisattvas.
The initial passage consists of four parts:

first, the establishment of the principle; second, the citation of an event beginning with "Śāriputra"; third, the existence of intention beginning with "Furthermore, the fourfold assembly"; and fourth, the existence of meaning beginning with "Faith and understanding."
